lec05kp09-u01-p1-title.name: u01-p1-title
lec05kp09-u01-p1-title.text: Squared error has two flaws: big errors drown small ones, and a confidently wrong output cannot learn

lec05kp09-u01-p1-bridge.name: u01-p1-bridge
lec05kp09-u01-p1-bridge.text: The speed-ups of KP08 all rewrite the update rule, but where the update goes depends on the cost function itself. What is wrong with the common squared error?

lec05kp09-u01-p1-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp09-loss
lec05kp09-u01-p1-fig1.text: Two losses against the output ŷ for target 1: the squared error is bounded by 0.5, the other loss −ln ŷ diverges as ŷ approaches 0, reaching 6.908 at ŷ=0.001.

image.alt: Two losses against the output ŷ for target 1: the squared error is bounded by 0.5, the other loss −ln ŷ diverges as ŷ approaches 0, reaching 6.908 at ŷ=0.001.

lec05kp09-u01-p1-c1.name: u01-p1-c1
lec05kp09-u01-p1-c1.text: **Unfair**: errors are squared before summing, so big errors dominate. Errors $0.9$ and $0.1$ differ 9 times, but squared they are $0.81$ and $0.01$, 81 times.

lec05kp09-u01-p1-c2.name: u01-p1-c2
lec05kp09-u01-p1-c2.text: **It can stall**: when the output $\hat y$ is wrong at an extreme (target 1, output $0.001$) the squared error is only $0.499$ and never grows; gradient descent can get stuck (source citing Witt 00).

lec05kp09-u01-p1-c3.name: u01-p1-c3
lec05kp09-u01-p1-c3.text: **Contrast**: another loss, $-\ln\hat y$, is $6.908$ at $\hat y=0.001$ and keeps growing the more wrong it is.

lec05kp09-u01-p2-title.name: u01-p2-title
lec05kp09-u01-p2-title.text: When the output is wrong at an extreme the squared-error δ goes to 0: only 0.000045 at net = −10

lec05kp09-u01-p2-bridge.name: u01-p2-bridge
lec05kp09-u01-p2-bridge.text: Squared error is only $0.499$ when the output is wrong at an extreme and never grows. Why does gradient descent stop learning?

lec05kp09-u01-p2-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp09-mse-delta
lec05kp09-u01-p2-fig1.text: The squared-error δ against the weighted sum net: a peak of 0.148 near net −0.7 and only 0.000045 at net=−10, with the confidently wrong region shaded.

image.alt: The squared-error δ against the weighted sum net: a peak of 0.148 near net −0.7 and only 0.000045 at net=−10, with the confidently wrong region shaded.

lec05kp09-u01-p2-term:高原.name: term:Plateau
lec05kp09-u01-p2-term:高原.text: **Plateau**: a flat region where the error is large but the gradient is almost 0, so gradient descent hardly moves on it.

lec05kp09-u01-p2-c1.name: u01-p2-c1
lec05kp09-u01-p2-c1.text: **Why**: for a single sigmoid output $\delta=(y-\hat y)\,\hat y(1-\hat y)$; the closer $\hat y$ is to 0 or 1 the smaller the slope $\hat y(1-\hat y)$, squeezing even a big error into a small signal.

lec05kp09-u01-p2-c2.name: u01-p2-c2
lec05kp09-u01-p2-c2.text: **Example** (target $y=1$): at $net=-10$, $\hat y=0.000045$, the error is almost 1 and $\delta=0.000045$.

lec05kp09-u01-p3-title.name: u01-p3-title
lec05kp09-u01-p3-title.text: Cross-entropy cancels the sigmoid slope: δ = y − ŷ, so the worse the error the harder the fix

lec05kp09-u01-p3-bridge.name: u01-p3-bridge
lec05kp09-u01-p3-bridge.text: The squared-error $\delta$ is squeezed to $0.000045$ by the sigmoid slope. Which cost keeps $\delta$ from being squeezed?

lec05kp09-u01-p3-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp09-delta-table
lec05kp09-u01-p3-fig1.text: ŷ, the squared-error δ and the cross-entropy δ at net −10, −5, −2, 0, 2 and 5; 0.00005 against 1.0000 at net=−10.

image.alt: ŷ, the squared-error δ and the cross-entropy δ at net −10, −5, −2, 0, 2 and 5; 0.00005 against 1.0000 at net=−10.

lec05kp09-u01-p3-term:交叉熵.name: term:Cross-entropy
lec05kp09-u01-p3-term:交叉熵.text: **Cross-entropy**: read the output $\hat y$ as the probability that the target is 1, $J=-\big(y\ln\hat y+(1-y)\ln(1-\hat y)\big)$; for $y=1$ it is $-\ln\hat y$.

lec05kp09-u01-p3-c1.name: u01-p3-c1
lec05kp09-u01-p3-c1.text: **Derivation**: $\partial J/\partial\hat y=-\tfrac{y}{\hat y}+\tfrac{1-y}{1-\hat y}=-\tfrac{y-\hat y}{\hat y(1-\hat y)}$; the sigmoid slope $\hat y(1-\hat y)$ cancels it: $\delta=y-\hat y$ (squared error $\tfrac12(y-\hat y)^2$ keeps a slope factor).

lec05kp09-u01-p3-c2.name: u01-p3-c2
lec05kp09-u01-p3-c2.text: **Example**: at $net=-10$ the squared-error $\delta=0.00005$ and the cross-entropy $\delta=1.0000$; at $net=0$ it is $0.125$ against $0.5$.

lec05kp09-u01-p4-title.name: u01-p4-title
lec05kp09-u01-p4-title.text: The same wrong start: cross-entropy gets all four right in 5 epochs, squared error needs 85

lec05kp09-u01-p4-bridge.name: u01-p4-bridge
lec05kp09-u01-p4-bridge.text: The cross-entropy $\delta$ is $1.0000$ at $net=-10$ and is not squeezed by the slope. Trained for real, how far apart are the two costs?

lec05kp09-u01-p4-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp09-train
lec05kp09-u01-p4-fig1.text: The output ŷ of the point x=2 against epochs: cross-entropy quickly rises above 0.5 and towards 1 while squared error lies near 0 and crosses 0.5 only near epoch 85.

image.alt: The output ŷ of the point x=2 against epochs: cross-entropy quickly rises above 0.5 and towards 1 while squared error lies near 0 and crosses 0.5 only near epoch 85.

lec05kp09-u01-p4-c1.name: u01-p4-c1
lec05kp09-u01-p4-c1.text: **Setup**: one sigmoid neuron $\hat y=\sigma(b+wx)$, four points $x=-2,-1,1,2$ with targets $0,0,1,1$; start $w=-3,b=0$ so all four are wrong; $\eta=0.5$, batch updates.

lec05kp09-u01-p4-c2.name: u01-p4-c2
lec05kp09-u01-p4-c2.text: **Result**: cross-entropy gets all four right in 5 epochs and squared error needs 85 (program). The figure shows the output of the point $x=2$: squared error first lies near 0 for dozens of epochs.

lec05kp09-u01-p4-c3.name: u01-p4-c3
lec05kp09-u01-p4-c3.text: **An honest note**: both costs end up classifying correctly; the difference is the speed from a very wrong start.

lec05kp09-u01-p5-title.name: u01-p5-title
lec05kp09-u01-p5-title.text: Cross-entropy is the negative log-likelihood: multiply the probability of every target, take −ln

lec05kp09-u01-p5-bridge.name: u01-p5-bridge
lec05kp09-u01-p5-bridge.text: Cross-entropy made 5 against 85 epochs from a very wrong start. Besides working well, what is the reasoning behind it?

lec05kp09-u01-p5-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp09-likelihood
lec05kp09-u01-p5-fig1.text: Outputs, probability of the target and −ln for four samples: the product is 0.4536 and the −ln values sum to 0.7905.

image.alt: Outputs, probability of the target and −ln for four samples: the product is 0.4536 and the −ln values sum to 0.7905.

lec05kp09-u01-p5-term:概似.name: term:Likelihood
lec05kp09-u01-p5-term:概似.text: **Likelihood**: the probability of seeing this data if the model is right; larger is better. Independent samples multiply.

lec05kp09-u01-p5-c1.name: u01-p5-c1
lec05kp09-u01-p5-c1.text: **Example**: outputs $0.9,0.8,0.3,0.1$ with targets $1,1,0,0$: the probability of each target is $0.9,0.8,0.7,0.9$, the product is $0.4536$ and $-\ln0.4536=0.7905$.

lec05kp09-u01-p5-c2.name: u01-p5-c2
lec05kp09-u01-p5-c2.text: **It matches**: the four cross-entropies $0.105+0.223+0.357+0.105=0.790$ add up to $-\ln$ of the product. Minimizing cross-entropy equals maximizing likelihood.

lec05kp09-u01-p6-title.name: u01-p6-title
lec05kp09-u01-p6-title.text: Several classes use softmax: the outputs sum to 1 and the backprop δ is still y − ŷ

lec05kp09-u01-p6-bridge.name: u01-p6-bridge
lec05kp09-u01-p6-bridge.text: Cross-entropy is the negative log-likelihood of outputs read as probabilities. With several classes, how can the outputs be forced to sum to 1?

lec05kp09-u01-p6-term:softmax.name: term:softmax
lec05kp09-u01-p6-term:softmax.text: **softmax**: $\hat y_k=\dfrac{e^{v_k}}{\sum_{k'}e^{v_{k'}}}$, every output lies between 0 and 1 and they sum to exactly 1.

lec05kp09-u01-p6-c2.name: u01-p6-c2
lec05kp09-u01-p6-c2.text: **A neat by-product**: $\delta_k=y_k-\hat y_k=(0.341,-0.242,-0.099)$, equal to numerical differences (program check); no slope factor is left.

lec05kp09-u01-p7-title.name: u01-p7-title
lec05kp09-u01-p7-title.text: Squared error fits every target: one outlier tilts the boundary

lec05kp09-u01-p7-bridge.name: u01-p7-bridge
lec05kp09-u01-p7-bridge.text: softmax with cross-entropy learns the outputs as probabilities. Classification only needs the largest, so is that learning too much?

lec05kp09-u01-p7-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp09-lsfit
lec05kp09-u01-p7-fig1.text: Seven one-dimensional points with an outlier at x=40: the squared-error line cuts at 1.40 and misclassifies x=1, sigmoid with cross-entropy cuts at 0 and gets all seven right.

image.alt: Seven one-dimensional points with an outlier at x=40: the squared-error line cuts at 1.40 and misclassifies x=1, sigmoid with cross-entropy cuts at 0 and gets all seven right.

lec05kp09-u01-p7-term:判別式學習.name: term:Discriminative learning
lec05kp09-u01-p7-term:判別式學習.text: **Discriminative learning**: since the goal is a low error rate, focus on the largest posterior and push the decision surface down.

lec05kp09-u01-p7-c1.name: u01-p7-c1
lec05kp09-u01-p7-c1.text: **Contrast** (designed here): class 0 at $x=-3,-2,-1$; class 1 at $1,2,3$ and an outlier at $40$. The squared-error line cuts at $1.40$ and misses $x=1$; sigmoid with cross-entropy cuts at $0$, all seven right.

lec05kp09-u01-p7-c2.name: u01-p7-c2
lec05kp09-u01-p7-c2.text: **Limits**: the contrast changes output and cost. The error rate is not differentiable; a smooth version risks local minima (source).

lec05kp09-u01-p8-title.name: u01-p8-title
lec05kp09-u01-p8-title.text: Bayesian training looks at a distribution of weights: more data sharpens it, but classifying integrates

lec05kp09-u01-p8-bridge.name: u01-p8-bridge
lec05kp09-u01-p8-bridge.text: Discriminative learning still pushes the error rate down with one set of weights. Can we avoid choosing one and look at a distribution of weights?

lec05kp09-u01-p8-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp09-posterior
lec05kp09-u01-p8-fig1.text: Distributions of the weight with n=0, 1, 5 and 20 samples, standard deviations 2, 0.894, 0.436 and 0.222, sharper each time with the mean approaching 1.5.

image.alt: Distributions of the weight with n=0, 1, 5 and 20 samples, standard deviations 2, 0.894, 0.436 and 0.222, sharper each time with the mean approaching 1.5.

lec05kp09-u01-p8-term:貝氏訓練.name: term:Bayesian training
lec05kp09-u01-p8-term:貝氏訓練.text: **Bayesian training**: the prior $p(w)$ is the guess about the weights before the data; Bayes' rule adds the data and gives the corrected posterior $p(w\mid Y)$.

lec05kp09-u01-p8-c1.name: u01-p8-c1
lec05kp09-u01-p8-c1.text: **Example** (designed here): prior sd 2, every sample says $w\approx1.5$ (noise sd 1). For $n=0,1,5,20$ the posterior sd is $2,\,0.894,\,0.436,\,0.222$ and the mean $0,\,1.2,\,1.43,\,1.48$.

lec05kp09-u01-p8-c2.name: u01-p8-c2
lec05kp09-u01-p8-c2.text: **Price**: classifying averages over all possible $w$, a costly high-dimensional integral; the source notes that replacing least squares often gives no real gain.

lec05kp09-u01-p9-title.name: u01-p9-title
lec05kp09-u01-p9-title.text: Extension: the more wrong the start, the slower squared error: 88141 epochs at w = −10

lec05kp09-u01-p9-bridge.name: u01-p9-bridge
lec05kp09-u01-p9-bridge.text: Bayesian training looks at a distribution of weights, another road. Back to squared error against cross-entropy: the start $w=-3$ of page 4 already differs 17 times, so how far apart are they if the start is even more wrong?

lec05kp09-u01-p9-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp09-init
lec05kp09-u01-p9-fig1.text: Log bar chart of the epochs needed from seven starts w=−1 to −10: 11 to 88141 for squared error and 2 to 14 for cross-entropy.

image.alt: Log bar chart of the epochs needed from seven starts w=−1 to −10: 11 to 88141 for squared error and 2 to 14 for cross-entropy.

lec05kp09-u01-p9-c1.name: u01-p9-c1
lec05kp09-u01-p9-c1.text: **Example** (the data of page 4 and $\eta=0.5$): from $w=-1,-2,-3,-4,-6,-8,-10$ squared error needs 11, 31, 85, 227, 1631, 11950 and 88141 epochs and cross-entropy only 2, 4, 5, 6, 9, 12 and 14.

lec05kp09-u01-p9-c2.name: u01-p9-c2
lec05kp09-u01-p9-c2.text: **How to read it**: the squared-error $\delta$ shrinks exponentially as the start gets worse, so the epochs grow roughly exponentially; the cross-entropy $\delta$ stays near 1 and the epochs grow slowly.

lec05kp09-u01-p10-title.name: u01-p10-title
lec05kp09-u01-p10-title.text: Extension: practice, how many times do the two δ differ at net = −4

lec05kp09-u01-p10-bridge.name: u01-p10-bridge
lec05kp09-u01-p10-bridge.text: The more wrong the start, the larger the gap between the two costs. Quantify it: at $net=-4$ with target 1, what are the two $\delta$?

lec05kp09-u01-p10-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp09-practice
lec05kp09-u01-p10-fig1.text: Practice figure: a single sigmoid output, target 1 and weighted sum net=−4; find the two δ and their ratio.

image.alt: Practice figure: a single sigmoid output, target 1 and weighted sum net=−4; find the two δ and their ratio.

lec05kp09-u01-p10-q2.name: u01-p10-q2
lec05kp09-u01-p10-q2.text: **Hint**: squared error $\delta=(1-\hat y)\,\hat y(1-\hat y)$, cross-entropy $\delta=1-\hat y$.

lec05kp09-u01-p10-q3.name: u01-p10-q3
lec05kp09-u01-p10-q3.text: **Question 2**: what are the two $\delta$ and how many times larger is the cross-entropy one?

lec05kp09-u01-p11-title.name: u01-p11-title
lec05kp09-u01-p11-title.text: Extension: worked solution of questions 1 and 2

lec05kp09-u01-p11-bridge.name: u01-p11-bridge
lec05kp09-u01-p11-bridge.text: The practice asked for the two $\delta$ at $net=-4$ and their ratio. Worked out in full, what are the answers?

lec05kp09-u01-p11-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp09-practice-sol
lec05kp09-u01-p11-fig1.text: ŷ=0.0180, squared-error δ=0.01735, cross-entropy δ=0.9820 and ratio 56.6.

image.alt: ŷ=0.0180, squared-error δ=0.01735, cross-entropy δ=0.9820 and ratio 56.6.

lec05kp09-u01-p11-a3.name: u01-p11-a3
lec05kp09-u01-p11-a3.text: **Check**: the ratio is exactly $1/[\hat y(1-\hat y)]=56.6$ and grows as the output gets more extreme; at $net=-10$ it is about 22000.

steps.label: Choosing the cost
steps.speakerNotes: Level: undergraduate (year 3). Main line 8 pages plus 3 extension pages (not timed). Self-study deck, English version. Made under CLARITY.md C12 to C18. It uses small examples: a single sigmoid output neuron on four one-dimensional points, an outlier example, a three-class softmax and a Gaussian posterior; every number was recomputed by a program and these small examples were designed for this lecture to show the mechanisms (added). The sign of delta is fixed as delta = -dJ/dnet (the source writes the cross-entropy delta as yhat - y, which differs by a sign). Speaker notes are published with the file and contain no student numbers, grades or exam items.

steps.label: Squared error's flaws
steps.speakerNotes: The speed-ups of KP08 all rewrite the update rule, but where the update goes depends on the cost function itself. This page asks what is wrong with the common squared error. The source lists two flaws. First it is unfair: errors are squared before summing so big errors dominate; errors of 0.9 and 0.1 differ 9 times but 0.81 and 0.01 differ 81 times. Second it can stall: when the output is wrong at an extreme, for example target 1 and output 0.001, the squared error is only 0.499 and no longer grows, so gradient descent may be stuck. The figure shows both losses against the output for target 1: the squared error is bounded while the other loss, minus ln of the output, diverges as the output approaches 0, reaching 6.908 at 0.001. The next page asks why squared error stops learning.

steps.label: The plateau
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said squared error stops growing when the output is wrong at an extreme. This page asks why gradient descent stops learning. One word first: a plateau is a flat region where the error is large but the gradient is almost 0. The cause is the delta of a single sigmoid output: target minus output, times the sigmoid slope, output times 1 minus output. The closer the output is to 0 or 1, the smaller the slope, which squeezes even a big error into a small signal. The figure shows delta against the weighted sum net for target 1: at net equal to minus 10 the output is 0.000045, the error is almost 1 and delta is only 0.000045. The next page tries a different cost function.

steps.label: Cross-entropy
steps.speakerNotes: On the previous page the squared-error delta was squeezed to 0.000045 by the sigmoid slope. This page switches to the cross-entropy: read the output as the probability that the target is 1; the cost is minus y times ln of the output plus 1 minus y times ln of 1 minus the output, which for target 1 is minus ln of the output. Derivation: the derivative of the cost with respect to the output is minus y minus output over output times 1 minus output; multiplied by the sigmoid slope, output times 1 minus output, it cancels exactly and gives delta equal to y minus output. The sign follows KP06, delta is the negative derivative, and the source writes output minus y, which differs by a sign. The table lists both deltas: at net minus 10 the squared error gives 0.00005 and the cross-entropy 1.0000. The next page looks at real training.

steps.label: Training compared
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page showed that the cross-entropy delta is 1.0000 at net minus 10 and is not squeezed by the slope. This page really trains: one sigmoid neuron, four points x equal to minus 2, minus 1, 1 and 2 with targets 0, 0, 1 and 1, starting weight minus 3 and bias 0 so all four are wrong, learning rate 0.5. Cross-entropy gets all four right in 5 epochs and squared error needs 85. The figure shows the output of the point x equal to 2: squared error first lies near 0 for dozens of epochs. Honestly, both costs end up classifying correctly; the difference is the speed from a very wrong start. The next page asks what the cross-entropy is the negative logarithm of.

steps.label: Likelihood
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page showed that cross-entropy made the two costs differ by 5 against 85 epochs from a very wrong start. This page asks what reasoning lies behind it besides working well. First likelihood: the probability of seeing this data if the model is right; independent samples multiply and larger is better. Example: four outputs 0.9, 0.8, 0.3 and 0.1 with targets 1, 1, 0 and 0 give the probabilities of the targets 0.9, 0.8, 0.7 and 0.9, whose product is 0.4536, and minus ln of it is 0.7905; the four cross-entropies 0.105, 0.223, 0.357 and 0.105 also add up to 0.790, so it matches. Minimizing the cross-entropy is therefore maximizing the likelihood. The next page extends the outputs to several classes.

steps.label: softmax
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page read the outputs as probabilities, so minimizing the cross-entropy maximizes the likelihood. This page asks how the outputs of several classes can be forced to sum to 1. The answer is to change the activation of the output layer to softmax: every output is e to the v divided by the sum of all e to the v, between 0 and 1 and summing to exactly 1. Example: v equal to (2, 1, 0.1) gives the outputs (0.659, 0.242, 0.099); with target (1, 0, 0) the cost is minus ln 0.659, which is 0.417. A neat by-product: the delta needed by backpropagation is exactly y minus the output, that is (0.341, minus 0.242, minus 0.099), which I verified with numerical differences; the source writes output minus y, which differs by a sign. The next page looks at another idea: lowering the classification error rate directly.

steps.label: Discriminative learning
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page learned the outputs as probabilities with softmax and cross-entropy. This page asks whether learning probabilities is learning too much, since classification only needs to know which is largest. The idea of discriminative learning is that, since the goal is a low classification error, the weight is put on the largest posterior directly. The contrast example was designed here to make it visible: x equal to minus 3, minus 2 and minus 1 are class 0, and x equal to 1, 2, 3 and the outlier x equal to 40 are class 1. The line fitted by squared error puts the boundary at 1.40 and misclassifies x equal to 1; sigmoid with cross-entropy puts it at 0 and gets all seven points right. To be honest, this contrast changes both the output and the cost; and the error rate itself is not differentiable, so a smooth version is used, with a risk of local minima. The next page looks from another angle: not one set of weights but a distribution over weights.

steps.label: Bayesian training
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page's discriminative learning still looks for one set of weights. This page asks whether we can avoid choosing one and look at a distribution of weights. Bayesian training sets a prior distribution on the weights and, once the data arrive, uses Bayes' rule to get the posterior. The example is designed here: prior standard deviation 2, every sample says w is about 1.5, noise standard deviation 1; with 0, 1, 5 and 20 samples the posterior standard deviation is 2, 0.894, 0.436 and 0.222 and the posterior mean 0, 1.2, 1.43 and 1.48, so more data gives a sharper distribution. The price is that classifying averages over all weights, an expensive high-dimensional integral; the source also reminds us that replacing least squares often brings no real gain in practice and the choice depends on the problem. The next extension page looks at how large the gap is from a very wrong start.

steps.label: Extension: worse starts
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page's Bayesian posterior only sharpens with more data, and the start of page 4 was only weight minus 3. This extension asks how far apart the two costs are if the start is even more wrong. With the same data and learning rate 0.5, starts of minus 1, minus 2, minus 3, minus 4, minus 6, minus 8 and minus 10 need 11, 31, 85, 227, 1631, 11950 and 88141 epochs with squared error and only 2, 4, 5, 6, 9, 12 and 14 with cross-entropy. The squared-error delta shrinks exponentially as the start gets worse, so the epochs grow roughly exponentially; the cross-entropy delta stays near 1. The next page poses an exercise.

steps.label: Extension: practice
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said the more wrong the start, the larger the gap between the two costs. This page quantifies it: a single sigmoid output, target 1 and weighted sum net equal to minus 4. Question 1: what is the output? Question 2: what are the two deltas and how many times larger is the cross-entropy one? The hint: the squared-error delta is 1 minus the output times the output times 1 minus the output; the cross-entropy delta is 1 minus the output. Work it out first, then see the next page.

steps.label: Extension: solution
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page posed the exercise and this page is the complete solution. Question 1: the output is 1 over 1 plus e to the 4, which is 0.0180. Question 2: the squared-error delta is 0.9820 times 0.0180 times 0.9820, which is 0.01735; the cross-entropy delta is 1 minus 0.0180, which is 0.9820; the ratio is 0.9820 over 0.01735, which is 56.6. Check: the ratio is exactly 1 over output times 1 minus output and grows as the output gets more extreme; at net minus 10 it is about 22000. That finishes the choice of the cost function; the next knowledge point looks at the choice of network size.
